title: Week 29 Check-In · By the Great Horn Spoon!
description: This week you read Chapters 13 to 15. You practiced sentence variety, the endings -ous, -ive and -ity, word families, how a writer builds voice and tone, every part of a poem at once, and revising your adventure for voice, dialogue and description. Show what you know.

questions.label: Identification
questions.text: Which sentence begins with a participial phrase?
options: Jack held on to Stubb.
Holding the rope tight, Jack waited.
When the dust cleared, a face appeared.
In the morning, they struck the tent.
questions.status: fixed (the old answer was an invented Ch. 15 sentence; a fourth option added)

questions.label: Vary the Length
questions.text: Rewrite this as two sentences, one short and one longer.
questions.excerpt: Jack walked around the burro and sized him up and then he spit in his hands and climbed on.
questions.key: Any two sentences, one short and one longer, e.g. Jack sized up the burro. Then he spit in his hands and climbed onto Stubb’s back.
questions.from: 29.1 Grammar (vary length); 29.2 Show What You Know
questions.status: changed (Ch. 14 events instead of the Ch. 15 coyote hole)

questions.label: Sentence Openers
questions.text: Which group of sentences starts its sentences in the most different ways?
options: Jack panned. Jack dug. Jack rested.
Jack panned all morning. After lunch, he dug. Tired at last, he rested.
Jack panned and dug and rested.
Jack panned, and Jack dug, and Jack rested.
questions.status: new (replaces a sentence-writing item; the scope's sentence variety)

questions.label: Suffix
questions.text: Which ending turns a word into a describing word that means full of?
options: -ity
-ous
-ive
-ment

questions.label: Word Meaning
options: Tending to avoid or escape
Full of courage
The state of being well known
A person who gives help
questions.status: changed (was 'use evasive in a sentence'; now multiple choice)

questions.label: Context Clues
questions.text: Read the line from Chapter 13. What does notoriety mean here?
questions.excerpt: The truth of the matter was that Praiseworthy himself began to enjoy his notoriety.
options: Being well known for something bold
Being very tired
Being afraid of crowds
Being good with money
questions.from: 29.1 Read Like a Writer; Vocabulary (notoriety, Ch. 13)

questions.label: Word Families
questions.text: Which word is NOT in the prospect family?
options: prospector
prospecting
prosperous
prospective
questions.status: fixed (the old item put prosperous in the prospect family)

questions.label: Build a Family
questions.text: Write three words in the create family. Underline the part that stays the same in all three.
questions.key: Any three of create, creation, creative, creator, creativity; the base creat stays the same.
questions.status: changed (the old item used the prospect family with prosperous)

questions.label: Spelling Shift
options: decidive
decisive
desicive
decisiv
questions.status: new (the d to s shift in a family)

questions.label: Key Detail
questions.text: Why does Praiseworthy call the bushel of neckties “a brilliant purchase”?
options: He plans to sell them when the miners want them, and buy a burro.
He wants to wear a different tie every day.
He thinks the auctioneer will give the money back.
He wants Jack to feel better, though he has no plan.

questions.label: Character and Tone
questions.text: Right after this, Praiseworthy says, “Put some beans on to fry, partner Jack. First thing in the morning we’ll start for Shirt-tail Camp.” What does this show about him? Answer in 2–3 sentences.
questions.key: He does not give up or dwell on the disappointment; he moves straight to the next plan, steady and hopeful, which keeps the book's tone light.
questions.status: fixed (the line is now quoted exactly; the passage is printed above it)

questions.label: Read Like a Writer
questions.text: In Chapter 15, Fleischman writes: “Yellow poppies had burst open on the hillsides like scatterings of fools’ gold.” What makes this strong description?
options: It names specific things and compares them to something from the gold fields.
It uses only very short sentences.
It tells exactly how many poppies there were.
It is a line of dialogue.
questions.status: new (the scope's Read Like a Writer focus: description)

questions.label: Poetry
questions.text: “Windy Nights” and “Fog” use the same five parts of a poem. How are they different?
options: Windy Nights gallops with rhyme and a strong beat; Fog is quiet, with short lines that do not rhyme.
Both poems rhyme in pairs.
Fog has a stronger beat than Windy Nights.
Windy Nights has no figurative language.

questions.label: Revise for Voice
questions.text: Copy one sentence from your adventure draft. Then rewrite it to improve its voice, its dialogue or its description, and name which one you improved.
questions.key: Original + a revised sentence that is clearly better in the named way (a storyteller's voice, dialogue that sounds like the character, or a specific detail).

passage.title: Reading passage (Chapter 15)
passage.text: Just as quickly Praiseworthy unclasped his knife and ripped open the lining. They laid open every inch of the coat. They examined and re-examined it, and Jack’s excitement died away. There was no map. There had never been a map sewn in the lining of the coat.
passage.cite: Sid Fleischman, By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 15
